summary:
FireWatch is a web-based historical burning activity explorer developed by Zenith DB for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It combines NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS active-fire detections with an interactive 3D globe, selectable study areas, and a year-by-month calendar.

Because the sensors have different detection characteristics, FireWatch places observations on a common 0.5° grid-cell-day basis and applies an experimental overlap-period median-ratio adjustment for historical comparison.
Users can explore seasonal peaks, compare months against historical baselines, inspect satellite records, examine a 2021 southwest Türkiye case study, and export scientific reports. We test the sensor adjustment on held-out years and display missing coverage and uncertainty.
FireWatch helps researchers, land managers, and educators understand historical burning patterns without claiming to predict wildfires, provide real-time emergency alerts, or deliver scientifically validated sensor equivalence.
details:
FireWatch — Historical Fire Intelligence

Team: Zenith DB
Lead Developer: dev_demir
Team Owner: Bahadır Albayrakoglu
Challenge: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots

Problem and Purpose

Wildfires, agricultural burns, and other intense thermal events have been detected by NASA satellites for more than two decades. However, MODIS and VIIRS have different spatial resolutions, detection sensitivities, and observation characteristics. Their raw detection counts cannot be directly interpreted as a single consistent historical record.

FireWatch addresses this challenge by making historical burning activity easier to explore, compare, and understand.

How FireWatch Works

FireWatch retrieves historical NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS active-fire observations and presents them through an interactive 3D globe and a historical burning activity calendar.

Users can select a supported country or define a rectangular area of interest, choose a year or date range, inspect satellite hotspot observations, and examine changes in burning activity over time.

To provide a common basis for comparison, the application aggregates detections into 0.5-degree geographic grid cells and UTC days. Multiple detections from the same sensor within one cell on the same day are counted as one active cell-day.

An experimental harmonization method estimates month-specific relationships between MODIS and VIIRS during their overlapping observation years. These relationships are used to create provisional VIIRS-like historical activity estimates where appropriate.

Key Features

  • Interactive 3D Earth with satellite imagery and geographic labels.
  • Clickable fire detections with available observation details, including coordinates, sensor, date, and Fire Radiative Power (FRP).
  • Multi-year burning activity calendar and selectable geographic study areas.
  • Raw MODIS, raw VIIRS, and experimentally adjusted MODIS comparison charts.
  • Historical seasonal patterns and anomaly analysis.
  • Chronological validation using held-out years and comparison-error metrics.
  • A southwest Türkiye 2021 historical fire activity case study.
  • Downloadable CSV results and reproducible scientific reports.
  • Independent NASA EONET named event references.

Innovation and Potential Impact

FireWatch combines geographic exploration with transparent historical analysis. Rather than displaying hotspots alone, it helps users understand how differences between satellite sensors can influence long-term comparisons.

Researchers, land managers, educators, and emergency-planning teams may use FireWatch to explore seasonal patterns, investigate historically unusual periods, and identify times when closer monitoring may be useful.

The application communicates uncertainty, missing observations, and source limitations alongside its analytical results.

Technology and Resources

FireWatch was developed with JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and Node.js serverless APIs. It uses CesiumJS for interactive 3D visualization, Esri mapping services for geographic imagery and labels, NASA FIRMS for historical MODIS and VIIRS observations, and NASA EONET for named natural-event references. The application is deployed on Vercel.

OpenAI ChatGPT was extensively used to assist with implementation, debugging, interface content, scientific analysis code, testing, and documentation. The team directed the project and is responsible for reviewing the implementation and interpreting the results.

Scientific Limitations

The MODIS–VIIRS harmonization method is experimental and has not been independently validated as a physical sensor calibration. It does not fully correct for cloud cover, satellite overpass timing, detection probability, or geographic differences in grid-cell area.

The global visualization uses a selected subset of country archives and does not represent complete worldwide fire coverage.

Active-fire detections are not equivalent to individual named wildfires, burned-area measurements, or exact ignition locations.

FireWatch is a historical research application, not a real-time wildfire warning system or a predictive emergency response tool.
